items.summary: Scientists tracked the changing sleep patterns of Indigenous people in Argentina who gained access to mains electricity — and smart phones.

items.summary: Nature staff discuss how precisely measuring a positron could shed light on one of physics’ greatest mysteries — plus, the latest on an ambitious mission to a Martian moon.

items.summary: Infectious-disease researchers say the risk of the livestock pathogen moving between people is low.

items.summary: What can a researcher in an overworked laboratory do to take care of themselves and their lab-mates, and how should they navigate medical disclosure?

items.summary: From underwater speakers to growing super-corals, scientists battle to save reefs around the world.

items.title: A first for CRISPR: powerful prime editing alters DNA directly in the human body
items.summary: Application of the high-precision technique is part of a clinical trial to treat a genetic disease that can cause liver and nerve damage.

items.title: Teen depression and anxiety predicted by childhood brain development
items.summary: Analysis of nearly 30,000 brain scans yields detailed timeline of how the brain matures — and hints at the consequences of disrupting it.

items.title: Can maths survive AI? Fields medallist Terence Tao calls for a ‘Maths 2.0’ world
items.summary: As machines race ahead in solving problems, mathematicians must establish a new era that prizes human understanding over simply publishing more solutions.

items.summary: See what gave Denisovans their distinct look. Plus, a vaccine trial for Ebola could kick off this week in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and what makes a great climate graphic.

items.summary: Author Correction: Catalyst-free, microdroplet-mediated waste plastic conversion to diacids

items.title: AI doctors’ orders come with a sky-high bill
items.summary: Large language models suggest more tests, referrals and medications than human physicians do, driving up the cost of care.

items.title: Surprise! White dwarf stars come in a rainbow of colours
items.summary: Analysis of some nearby stars shows that, despite their name, these bodies can be pink, yellow and more.

items.title: To heal sick cities, scientists and residents must work together
items.summary: Tolullah Oni has developed a platform to transfer the intellectual capital of African diaspora scholars back to the continent.

items.title: An AI tool improves weather forecasts up to a month ahead
items.summary: An innovative artificial-intelligence application enhances weather forecasting in the difficult subseasonal range, providing accurate forecasts of precipitation, temperature and pressure 3–5 weeks in advance. The tool refines both physics- and AI-based weather models and improves the early prediction of extremes of heat, cold, rainfall and flooding.

items.title: Using AI to offer personalized health advice
items.summary: The use of artificial-intelligence tools in medicine is increasing. What types of technology might be on the horizon and how can such health-advice tools be tested?

items.title: Global emissions slow — but world hurtles towards 2 °C of warming
items.summary: The United Nations’ latest climate report is a stark reminder that limiting warming to the safest levels is now likely to be out of reach.

items.title: Huge mapping study reveals how your brain tracks what your body is feeling
items.summary: Signals in the insula region, deep in the brain, can make people feel hot, tingly and nauseous.

items.title: Plastics embedded with enzymes degrade readily in the sea
items.summary: Embedding enzymes that break down ester bonds into compostable polyesters enables rapid and complete biodegradation even in microbe-scarce environments. This method is effective in marine sites ranging from coastal sea water to the deep sea, and could therefore contribute towards solving the global plastic pollution problem.

items.title: The Bursar
items.summary: A good way to learn?

items.title: This is what the mysterious Denisovans looked like
items.summary: Archaeologists identified skull fragments from China as belonging to this group of ancient human relatives.

items.title: Can plants defend coasts against storms?
items.summary: Salt-marsh plants can protect inland areas against huge waves — but seemingly only up to a point, and big storms cause progressive damage.

items.title: Worms live longer in cool conditions thanks to a muscle-derived molecule
items.summary: In nematodes, a metabolite induced by the cold links low temperatures to a body-wide signal that promotes longevity. This signalling system is also seen in human cells.

items.title: Daily briefing: How tech billionaires are changing science funding
items.summary: Ultra-rich philanthropists are disrupting biomedical science. Plus, why physicists have kept an antimatter particle caged for months and whether it’s really possible to be swallowed by a whale and survive.

items.title: Cave stalagmites document global patterns in monsoon rainfall over the past 450,000 years
items.summary: A 450,000-year stalagmite record of rainfall in the Amazon Basin , combined with existing Asian records, shows that the global monsoon system has oscillated regularly, strengthening in one hemisphere while weakening in the other. However, during intervals of warmth and warming climate, monsoons in both hemispheres failed for millennia.

items.title: Large-scale single crystals printed layer by layer
items.summary: A 3D-printing method has made single crystals of metals and alloys in complex shapes and up to one metre in length, as needed for advanced technological applications.

items.title: A single antimatter particle in a cage opens door to ‘revolutionary’ physics
items.summary: Physicists trap and cool down positron for months to measure its ‘magnetic moment’ with extraordinary precision.

items.title: Robert Williamson obituary: geneticist who mapped genes for muscular dystrophy and cystic fibrosis
items.summary: Researcher and policy adviser who championed tests and treatments for genetic diseases.

items.title: Fabric user interface can be worn on your sleeve — and machine-washed
items.summary: Touch-sensitive, light-emitting yarn can turn everyday clothing into washable, bendable user interfaces with dynamic graphics and versatile computing functions.

items.title: How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science
items.summary: Money from the world’s increasingly prosperous technology entrepreneurs has been flooding into biomedical research. Is it changing how science is done?

items.title: How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact
items.summary: Tech entrepreneurs are bringing an engineer’s eye to research funding. They must be open about their findings to reap maximum benefit.

items.title: Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation
items.summary: Now that hyperacute rejection of pig xenografts can be reliably prevented, subtler immune-mediated graft injuries have emerged that conventional diagnostics often miss; a multimodal precision diagnostic framework is proposed to detect these injuries earlier, guide personalized immunosuppression and inform future gene editing strategies.

items.title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms
items.summary: Salt marsh platforms resist erosion under extreme waves, but vegetation damage reduces wave attenuation; substantial wave attenuation by vegetation is mainly limited to low-energy marsh coasts with waves below 1 m.

items.title: Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement
items.summary: The use of zeolites with an appropriate pore structure combined with a high CO/olefin ratio is shown to catalyse olefin carbonylation and produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products.

items.title: Cold activates a BH2 metabolic network promoting longevity and proteostasis
items.summary: A multi-tissue signalling system links cold temperature to enhanced longevity and proteostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans.

items.title: WEE1 opposes APC/C<sup>CDH1</sup> activity to promote S phase entry
items.summary: Experimental and modelling data indicate that WEE1 promotes re-entry of quiescent cells into the cell cycle, potentially explaining the toxic side effects of WEE1 inhibitors in cancer therapies.

items.title: A single archaeon couples long-chain fatty acid oxidation to methanogenesis
items.summary: Methanoglobus dolicholipophagus AA-75 is a thermophilic archaeon isolated from a Chinese petroleum reservoir that converts methanol into methane, carbon dioxide and acetate, and uses saturated and unsaturated fatty acids to produce methane.

items.title: An environmentally regulated dichotomy in cell lineages of the root
items.summary: An environment-regulated state is identified across multiple cell types at the root tip, revealing a shared dichotomy between cells with and without this state.

items.title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits
items.summary: CD51+ astrocytes promote synapse formation in the developing cortex, circuit plasticity in the hippocampus and circuit remodelling after stroke.
